headline: High: shared filesystem and broad egress create dangerous write/conflict and data-flow risks; TREK’s MCP/browser surface amplifies cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Plandex reads and writes a project directory with review-then-apply, while TREK exposes MCP and browser-driven workflows. If TREK content is routed into Plandex files or prompts, instruction-like text can be misread. The pair lacks explicit provenance isolation, so the interaction is plausible in default setups.
conditions: IF TREK content is copied into Plandex-managed files or prompts, injection is possible.
IF MCP payloads from TREK are treated as trusted instructions by Plandex, hijack risk increases.
mitigations: Disable auto-apply in Plandex.
Keep TREK outputs out of Plandex prompt inputs.
Use separate workspaces for the two agents.
Add a manual review step before any file-based handoff.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Plandex has broad network egress and handles model-provider API keys, while TREK touches reservations, documents, API keys, and MFA secrets. If they share a workspace or operator account, sensitive travel data can flow into Plandex context and then out via its external calls. The profiles do not show isolation strong enough to rule this out.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same filesystem or copied files, leakage risk exists.
IF TREK secrets or reservation data are pasted into Plandex prompts, they may be transmitted externally.
mitigations: Keep TREK secrets out of Plandex inputs.
Use separate OS users or containers.
Redact reservation numbers and API keys before handoff.
Restrict Plandex network access during sensitive work.
Review logs in TREK for accidental secret capture.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Plandex can write the filesystem and modify git state; TREK is collaborative and uses files plus WebSocket/MCP-backed state. Shared mutable resources with no locking are a direct conflict pathway, and Plandex’s per-plan shared backend increases the chance of concurrent edits. This is dangerous by default because both can mutate overlapping state.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same repository or data directory, conflicts can occur.
IF TREK and Plandex edit shared files without external locking, last-writer-wins corruption is possible.
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories to each agent.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Use git locks or a single-writer workflow.
Snapshot files before concurrent edits.
Avoid simultaneous MCP and filesystem writes.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Plandex uses a review-then-apply workflow, but TREK is a real-time collaborative planner with AI built in and browser/MCP surfaces. If TREK consumes Plandex-generated plans or facts without verification, errors can cascade into user-visible travel actions. The review step lowers risk, but not enough to make the pathway low.
conditions: IF TREK treats Plandex output as authoritative, downstream mistakes can propagate.
IF Plandex auto-apply is enabled and TREK ingests the result, errors can cascade faster.
mitigations: Require human verification of Plandex outputs before TREK uses them.
Disable Plandex auto-apply.
Add schema checks on exchanged data.
Limit handoff to summaries, not raw plans.
Log and diff every transferred artifact.

E_compliance.rationale: Plandex handles source code and model-provider keys, while TREK handles reservations, country visit history, email addresses, and MFA secrets. If travel PII is processed through Plandex’s external model path or logs, the pair can create a compliance mismatch around retention and residency. The profiles do not prove a specific jurisdiction, so I choose medium rather than low due to the sensitive data mix.
conditions: IF EU travel PII is routed through Plandex model-provider calls, residency/compliance issues may arise.
IF TREK logs reservation or identity data into shared files, retention obligations may be violated.
mitigations: Keep PII out of Plandex prompts.
Separate logs for code and travel data.
Apply retention limits to TREK logs.
Use a DPA-approved model path for any personal data.
Redact country visit history before transfer.
